title: 慢旅行 vs 打卡式旅行
title_en: Why Slow Travel Leaves You with More to Say
summary_zh: 八天五座城、清单逐项打勾，回来却只记得排队。作者为“慢旅行”辩护，也公平地承认打卡式旅行的道理——一篇有立场、有让步的观点文，示范了高级论证的写法。
body: There is a particular kind of exhaustion that only a well-planned holiday can produce. You know the type: five cities in eight days, alarms set for dawn, and a list of landmarks crossed off with grim satisfaction on the train to the next place. Measured by the number of sights seen, such a trip is a triumph. Measured by what you actually remember, it is often a blur of queues, station platforms and the backs of other tourists' heads. Slow travel starts from a different question. Rather than asking how much of a place you can see, it asks how well you can come to know a small part of it. That might mean staying a week in a single town, shopping at the same market until the stallholders recognise you, or returning to one bakery so often that your order is being wrapped before you have finished saying it. None of this is glamorous, and it rarely makes for dramatic photographs. Yet it is precisely in these repeated, unremarkable moments that a place stops being scenery and starts to feel lived in. To be fair, the checklist approach has its defenders, and they are not entirely wrong. Not everyone has the luxury of unlimited time, and for someone who may visit a country only once, wanting to see its most famous sights is hardly unreasonable. Neither the rushed tourist nor the slow traveller holds a monopoly on meaningful experience. But I suspect many of us rush less out of genuine curiosity than out of a fear of missing out, as if an unvisited museum were a personal failure. If we treated a trip less like an exam to be passed and more like a conversation to be continued, we might return home less tired and, oddly, with more to say. The sights, after all, will outlast us. The chance to sit still somewhere unfamiliar and simply pay attention is rarer, and far easier to waste.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main argument?
options: Seeing famous sights is a waste of a traveller's time
Getting to know one place slowly often gives a richer experience
People should visit each country only once in their lives
Slow travel is mainly a cheaper way to see the world
questions.evidence: it is precisely in these repeated, unremarkable moments that a place stops being scenery and starts to feel lived in

questions.prompt: What does "a blur of queues" suggest about a rushed trip?
options: The traveller remembers every detail clearly
The memories are unclear and run together
The queues were shorter than expected
The photos from the trip are badly focused
questions.evidence: it is often a blur of queues, station platforms and the backs of other tourists' heads

questions.prompt: What does the writer mean by treating a trip "more like a conversation to be continued"?
options: Trips should always be repeated every year
Travellers should talk more on trains
Travel should build a connection with a place over time
Every trip should be planned in detail
questions.evidence: more like a conversation to be continued

questions.prompt: What reason does the writer give for why many of us rush when we travel?
options: A fear of missing out
Bad weather
Cheap train tickets
Short opening hours
questions.evidence: out of a fear of missing out

vocabulary.example: The small local festival turned out to be a triumph.
Working as a tour guide sounds glamorous, but the hours are long.
From the outside, the restaurant looked completely unremarkable.
No single city has a monopoly on good food.

vocabulary.meaning: 比……更持久；比……存在得更久
vocabulary.example: These old stone bridges will outlast all of us.

expressions.note: cross sth off a list 指完成一项就划掉一项，用来描写“打卡式”旅行非常传神。

expressions.meaning: 模糊成一片的……；记不清的一堆……
expressions.note: 形容经历太快、太满以至于记不清：The whole week was a blur of meetings.
make for + 名词，常说 make for a good story / a relaxing evening。
让步时的常用开头，先承认对方观点有道理，再继续自己的论证，显得客观。
比喻用法，多用于否定：No one holds a monopoly on good ideas.

expressions.text: less out of genuine curiosity than out of a fear of missing out
expressions.meaning: 与其说出于真正的好奇，不如说是怕错过
expressions.note: less out of A than out of B 用来分析真实动机；fear of missing out 就是常说的 FOMO。

knowledge.quote: If we treated a trip less like an exam to be passed and more like a conversation to be continued, we might return home less tired
knowledge.explanation: 与现在事实相反（我们现在并没有这样对待旅行）：if + 一般过去时，主句 might + 动词原形。用 might 而非 would，语气更谨慎，适合提出设想。

knowledge.quote: Neither the rushed tourist nor the slow traveller holds a monopoly on meaningful experience.
knowledge.explanation: neither ... nor ... 连接两个主语时，谓语与靠近的那个主语一致：the slow traveller 是单数，所以用 holds。

knowledge.quote: Measured by the number of sights seen, such a trip is a triumph.
knowledge.explanation: 过去分词短语 Measured by ... 作状语，逻辑主语是 such a trip（旅行“被衡量”）；sights seen 里的 seen 是后置过去分词。下一句重复 Measured by，形成鲜明对比。

speaking: 用 1 分钟说说你更喜欢“慢旅行”还是“打卡式旅行”，并承认另一种方式的一个优点，用上 To be fair 和 makes for。
writing: 用 180–220 词写一篇观点短文：旅行应该求“多”还是求“深”？至少有一处让步，用上 Neither ... nor ... 和一个 If we ..., we might ... 的虚拟句。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 less out of ... than out of ... 分析你或身边的人做某件事的真实动机。
task.model: many of us rush less out of genuine curiosity than out of a fear of missing out

title: 我们真正带回家的是什么
title_en: What We Really Bring Home: The Quiet Power of Souvenirs
summary_zh: 冰箱贴、木雕大象、没人记得买过的水晶球——纪念品常被嫌弃，但它们真正承载的是记忆。作者还提出：最好的纪念品也许根本不是“东西”，而是一个习惯、一句话。
body: Almost every home contains a small museum of other places: a fridge magnet shaped like a lighthouse, a carved wooden elephant, a snow globe that nobody remembers buying. We tend to think of souvenirs as faintly embarrassing, the kind of thing sold in identical shops beside every famous view. Yet the urge to carry something back is remarkably persistent, and it says something about how memory works. What we actually bring home is rarely the object itself. A cheap ceramic bowl is worth very little on a shelf, but it can return you, in an instant, to the hot afternoon when you bargained for it in a language you barely spoke. The object works less like a trophy than like a key, unlocking a scene that would otherwise fade. This is why the most treasured souvenirs are so often things no shop would bother to sell: a ticket stub, a pebble from a particular beach, a recipe scribbled by a host whose handwriting you can still picture. Their value lies in the story attached to them, which is invisible to anyone else. The meaning of such objects has little to do with what they cost or how well they were made. Some travellers go further and argue that the best souvenirs are not things at all. A new habit, such as an afternoon rest or a different way of making coffee, can travel home in your head and quietly reshape your days. So can a single phrase picked up from a stranger and repeated so often that your friends start using it too. None of this means the fridge magnet deserves our scorn. Even the most ordinary object, chosen at the end of a good trip, can punch above its weight. The question worth asking before we buy is simply whether it will remind us of something we want to keep.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the article?
options: Souvenirs sold near famous sights are usually poor value
Souvenirs matter mainly because of the memories they hold
Travellers should stop buying mass-produced souvenirs
Handmade souvenirs are always better than shop-bought ones
questions.evidence: Their value lies in the story attached to them, which is invisible to anyone else.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer compare a souvenir to "a key"?
options: It opens up a memory that might otherwise be lost
Souvenirs are often kept in locked boxes at home
It proves to others that you visited a famous place
It is small, light and easy to carry home
questions.evidence: unlocking a scene that would otherwise fade

questions.prompt: What does "punch above its weight" mean in "can punch above its weight"?
options: be heavier than it looks
have more effect or value than you would expect
break easily
cost more than it should

questions.prompt: According to the writer, what kind of souvenir can travel home "in your head"?
options: A snow globe
A new habit, such as an afternoon rest
A fridge magnet
A carved wooden elephant
questions.evidence: A new habit, such as an afternoon rest or a different way of making coffee, can travel home in your head

vocabulary.example: There was a persistent smell of smoke in the kitchen.
She bargained with the seller until they both started laughing.
This old camera is one of my most treasured possessions.
A year abroad can reshape the way you see your own country.
He talked about tourist shops with open scorn.

expressions.note: 委婉地表示某个现象透露出更深的东西：The way you pack says something about you.
= instantly，但更有画面感，写作和口语都常用。

expressions.text: less like a trophy than like a key
expressions.meaning: 与其说像奖杯，不如说像钥匙
expressions.note: less A than B 用来纠正常见看法；这里用两个比喻对照，很适合仿写。
have nothing / little / a lot to do with 是议论文高频表达。
pick up 指不刻意地学会语言、习惯、口音：I picked up a few words from the taxi driver.

expressions.meaning: 作用远超其分量；以小博大
expressions.note: 源自拳击，指小个子打赢大个子；媒体和评论里常用来夸“小东西有大作用”。

knowledge.quote: What we actually bring home is rarely the object itself.
knowledge.explanation: What 引导主语从句（“我们真正带回家的东西”），整个从句当作单数主语，谓语用 is。What ... is ... 句式能把真正的重点放在句末。

knowledge.quote: The meaning of such objects has little to do with what they cost or how well they were made.
knowledge.explanation: 主语中心词是 meaning（单数），of such objects 只是修饰语，所以谓语用 has，而不是被 objects 带成 have。

knowledge.quote: a recipe scribbled by a host whose handwriting you can still picture
knowledge.explanation: whose 引导定语从句表示所属关系（“那位房东的笔迹”）；whose + 名词在从句里作 picture 的宾语。前面的 scribbled by ... 是过去分词作后置定语。

speaking: 用 1 分钟介绍一件你珍藏的纪念品或旧物，说说它让你想起了什么，用上 in an instant 和 has little to do with。
writing: 用 150–200 词写一篇短文：你从一次旅行或一段经历中“带回”的、不是物品的东西是什么？用上 What I ... is ... 和 less like ... than like ...。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 What we actually ... is rarely ... 写一句关于学习、工作或旅行的“真相”。
task.model: What we actually bring home is rarely the object itself.

title: 寄宿家庭的“空盘子”误会
title_en: The Empty Plate: A Homestay Misunderstanding
summary_zh: Olu 从小被教导“吃光才礼貌”，寄宿家庭却认为“盘子空了就是还饿”——于是每晚的饭越添越多。一个温暖好笑的故事，讲习惯之间的误会，以及“开口问”的价值。
body: For the first week of his language course, Olu was quietly convinced that his host family was trying to fatten him up. Every evening, Astrid, his host mother, would set down a generous plate of stew, and every evening Olu would work his way through it, determined not to leave a single bite. His grandmother had raised him to believe that an unfinished plate was an insult to the cook, and he was not about to insult a woman who had welcomed a stranger into her home. The trouble was that the moment his fork touched an empty plate, Astrid would smile, say something warm that he couldn't quite follow, and fill it again. By the fourth night he was eating what amounted to two dinners and sleeping badly. Too polite to refuse and too proud to admit he didn't understand, he began skipping lunch to make room. It was Astrid's youngest son, Nils, who finally solved the mystery. Watching Olu struggle through a third helping of potatoes, the boy leaned across the table and whispered, in careful English, that in their house an empty plate meant only one thing: the guest was still hungry. Olu stared at him, then at the potatoes, and burst out laughing so hard that the whole family joined in without knowing why. Once Nils had translated, Astrid laughed even harder and confessed that she had been secretly alarmed by how much he seemed to need. Looking back, Olu finds the episode both comic and oddly instructive. Each of them was following a rule so familiar that it no longer felt like a rule at all. Had he simply asked on the first night, he wouldn't now be remembered in that household as the boy who ate two dinners. Then again, he suspects he would never have learned, quite so vividly, that kindness can speak in two different dialects, and that the only way to understand either is to ask.

questions.prompt: What was the real cause of the problem at dinner?
options: Astrid believed Olu disliked her cooking
Olu and Astrid followed different unspoken rules about empty plates
Olu was too shy to speak any English at the table
Nils played a joke on Olu during dinner
questions.evidence: Each of them was following a rule so familiar that it no longer felt like a rule at all.

questions.prompt: Why did Olu start skipping lunch?
options: He wanted to save money during the course
He had extra classes at lunchtime
He needed to leave space for the huge dinners
Astrid told him lunch was not included
questions.evidence: he began skipping lunch to make room

questions.prompt: Why did the whole family laugh "without knowing why"?
options: They were laughing at Olu's accent
Astrid had dropped the potatoes
Nils had told a joke in English
Olu's laughter spread before anyone understood the joke
questions.evidence: burst out laughing so hard that the whole family joined in without knowing why

questions.prompt: What does "instructive" mean in "both comic and oddly instructive"?
options: confusing
teaching something useful
embarrassing
boring

vocabulary.example: I was convinced that I had locked the door, but I hadn't.
The little restaurant is famous for its generous portions.

vocabulary.meaning: 有启发的；有教育意义的
vocabulary.example: Watching the chef work was more instructive than reading any recipe.
I still remember that first train journey vividly.
Many villages in the region have their own dialects.

expressions.note: fatten sb up 口语，带幽默，常用来说长辈拼命给孩子添饭。
work one's way through + 食物 / 书 / 工作，强调过程费劲：I'm working my way through a long reading list.
be not about to do 表示坚决不做某事，语气比 won't 更强。
本文是幽默用法：为晚饭腾出胃口。make room for sth 也可指时间、空间。
用在日常小事上带一点幽默，让叙述更生动。
burst out + doing 表示突然爆发，也可以说 burst out crying。

knowledge.quote: Had he simply asked on the first night, he wouldn't now be remembered in that household as the boy who ate two dinners.
knowledge.explanation: 倒装的错综条件：Had he asked 说过去（当时没问），wouldn't now be remembered 说现在的结果。主句里的 now 点明时间，是错综条件的标志。

knowledge.quote: His grandmother had raised him to believe that an unfinished plate was an insult to the cook
knowledge.explanation: 过去完成时 had raised 表示“过去的过去”：早在这次寄宿之前，奶奶就这样教他，为后面的误会埋下伏笔。

knowledge.quote: Each of them was following a rule so familiar that it no longer felt like a rule at all.
knowledge.explanation: Each of them 作主语时谓语用单数 was，尽管 them 是复数。each / either / neither of + 复数名词，都按单数处理。

speaking: 用 1 分钟讲一次你和别人因为习惯不同而产生的误会（在家里、学校或旅行中都可以），用上 was not about to 和 Looking back。
writing: 用 150–200 词写一个由“好意”引起的误会故事，结尾写你学到了什么，用上过去完成时和一个 Had I ..., I wouldn't now ... 的错综条件句。

task.prompt: 仿照这句错综条件（倒装 Had ..., ... wouldn't now ...），写一件你过去没做、导致现在某种结果的事。
task.model: Had he simply asked on the first night, he wouldn't now be remembered in that household as the boy who ate two dinners.

title: 旅行中拍当地人的礼仪
title_en: Ask Before You Shoot: The Etiquette of Photographing Locals
summary_zh: 一位旅行摄影师谈拍摄陌生人的分寸：先问再拍，语言不通就用表情询问，尊重每个地方的不成文规矩。读完你会知道，好照片和尊重并不矛盾。
body: Interviewer: You've spent years photographing people in markets, villages and city streets. What's the first rule you would give a traveller with a camera? Mariana: Ask before you shoot, which sounds obvious, but it's the rule people break most often, usually without meaning to. They see a striking face or a colourful stall, and the camera is up before they've even said hello. Interviewer: Doesn't asking ruin the moment, though, since the natural expression disappears as soon as someone knows they're being photographed? Mariana: Sometimes it does, and I've made my peace with that. A slightly stiff portrait of someone who agreed to it is worth far more to me than a perfect one taken from behind a pillar. Besides, if you stay a while, chat and perhaps buy something, people relax again, and the picture you get twenty minutes later is often better than the one you would have stolen. Interviewer: What if you don't share a language with the person? Mariana: Then you ask with your face and your hands: lift the camera slightly, raise your eyebrows and wait. If someone shakes their head or turns away, you should lower it, smile and move on, because no photograph is worth making a person feel like an exhibit. Interviewer: Are there situations where you wouldn't take pictures at all? Mariana: Every village and every market has its own unwritten rules, so I spend time watching how local people behave before I do anything. I never photograph children unless a parent is right there and has clearly said yes, and I'm wary of anyone in a vulnerable moment, however striking the image might be. Interviewer: Do you ever show people the results? Mariana: Whenever I can, because turning the screen around is the simplest way to share a moment rather than simply take it. People laugh, point at their friends and ask for another one, and occasionally they end up taking my photo instead, which seems only fair.

questions.prompt: What is Mariana's overall attitude to photographing local people?
options: A great photo matters more than how people feel
Respect for the person comes before getting the shot
Travellers should avoid photographing people at all
Only professional photographers should take portraits
questions.evidence: no photograph is worth making a person feel like an exhibit

questions.prompt: According to Mariana, why can staying a while lead to a better photo?
options: The light usually improves later in the day
People relax once you have spent some time with them
Local people prefer posing for professionals
Stolen photos are usually out of focus
questions.evidence: if you stay a while, chat and perhaps buy something, people relax again

questions.prompt: What does Mariana mean by not making a person "feel like an exhibit"?
options: Museums should not display photographs
People should not be treated as objects to be looked at
Exhibitions are too expensive to visit
Portraits belong only in galleries
questions.evidence: no photograph is worth making a person feel like an exhibit

questions.prompt: What does "wary" mean in "I'm wary of anyone in a vulnerable moment"?
options: excited
unaware
cautious and careful
jealous
questions.evidence: I'm wary of anyone in a vulnerable moment

vocabulary.example: She runs a small fruit stall near the station.
Everyone looked a bit stiff in the old family photo.
The oldest exhibit in the museum is a wooden boat.
Our cat is always wary of strangers at first.
People can feel vulnerable when they are far from home.

expressions.note: mean to do 表示“有意做”，否定形式常用来替人开脱：Sorry, I didn't mean to wake you.
make (one's) peace with sth 指接受无法改变的事，语气平和成熟。
形容被围观、被当成物件的感觉，非常形象。
中性说法，指大家默认遵守、却没人写下来的习惯。
be wary of sb / sth 表示保持戒心、不轻易行动。
句末用 which 评论前面整件事；only fair 表示“理所应当”，带一点幽默。

knowledge.quote: I never photograph children unless a parent is right there and has clearly said yes
knowledge.explanation: unless 引导条件，“除非家长在场并明确同意，否则绝不拍”。never ... unless ... 是表达个人原则的有力句式。

knowledge.quote: Every village and every market has its own unwritten rules
knowledge.explanation: every A and every B 作主语时，强调逐个看待，谓语仍用单数 has，代词也用 its 而不是 their。

knowledge.quote: If someone shakes their head or turns away, you should lower it, smile and move on
knowledge.explanation: 条件句的主句用情态动词 should 给出建议，if 从句用一般现在时。讲规矩、给指导时，“条件 + 情态动词”最常用。

speaking: 用 1 分钟说说你旅行时会不会拍陌生人、你的原则是什么，用上 unless 和 I'm wary of。
writing: 用 150–200 词为旅行者写一份“拍摄当地人礼仪”小指南，至少 3 条建议，用上 unwritten rules 和一个 never ... unless ... 句。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 I never ... unless ... 说一条你自己坚持的原则。
task.model: I never photograph children unless a parent is right there and has clearly said yes
